subject: english-literature
topicDisplay: Unit 4 Internal Assessment Comparative And Contextual Study
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: The risk of 'over-contextualising' a text is that:
options: The essay becomes too short
Context can never be excessive
Historical detail crowds out close reading, so the text itself is neglected
The analysis becomes too close to the words on the page
questions.explain: Excessive context can swamp engagement with the actual language and effects of the text.

questions.q: A nuanced view of the relationship between literature and its period holds that texts:
options: Merely passively mirror their society
Both reflect their context and can question, resist or reshape it
Can only ever endorse the values of their time
Are wholly untouched by history
questions.explain: Literature does not just mirror its age; it can also critique, subvert or intervene in it.

questions.q: The most sophisticated use of AO3 demonstrates that context can affect:
options: Neither meaning nor interpretation
Only the length of the text
Only the author's intentions
Both the meaning a text generated when produced and the varied meanings readers find across time
questions.explain: Advanced contextual study links context to production and to shifting reception, enriching interpretation.

questions.q: 'Texts in shared contexts' asks students to study works grouped by a common:
options: Author surname
Publisher
Page count
Social, historical or political context such as WWI or the changing role of women
questions.explain: The component clusters texts around a shared context, exploring how period and society shape literature.

questions.q: A 'motif' differs from a 'symbol' in that a motif is:
options: always a physical object
a recurring image, idea or device whose repetition builds significance across a text
a single image used only once for emphasis
a figure of speech comparing two unlike things
questions.explain: A motif gains its meaning through recurrence, whereas a symbol stands for something beyond itself at the point of use.

questions.q: A Marxist-influenced contextual reading would foreground a text's engagement with:
options: Class, power, labour and economic relations within the society depicted
The author's eye colour
Only the weather imagery
Rhyme and metre exclusively
questions.explain: Marxist criticism attends to class conflict, power and the material/economic conditions a text reflects or critiques.

questions.q: AO2 is best satisfied when a student:
options: lists the events of the plot in order
analyses how specific choices of form, structure and language create meaning and effect
summarises three critics' opinions
describes the writer's life and times
questions.explain: AO2 rewards close analysis of the writer's craft and the effects of formal, structural and linguistic choices.

questions.q: The 'connotation' of a word is:
options: its position in the sentence
its number of syllables
the associations and overtones it carries beyond its literal sense
its literal dictionary definition
questions.explain: Connotation refers to the implied associations a word evokes, as opposed to its denotative literal meaning.

questions.q: A 'feminist' reading of a canonical play would most characteristically interrogate:
options: the iambic substitutions in the verse
how the text constructs, constrains or resists gender roles and female agency
the rules of classical unity
the unconscious of the playwright alone
questions.explain: Feminist criticism examines representations of gender, patriarchal structures and the agency afforded to women in the text.

questions.q: 'Foregrounding' in stylistic analysis means:
options: describing the background setting
summarising the plot's opening
making a linguistic feature prominent through deviation or repetition so it draws attention
placing a scene at the front of the play
questions.explain: Foregrounding makes language conspicuous through patterning or deviation, directing the reader's interpretive attention.

questions.q: Post-colonial writing typically engages with:
options: The legacies of colonialism, including identity, displacement, language and the contesting of imperial narratives
The glorification of empire
Medieval courtly love
The natural sciences only
questions.explain: Post-colonial literature interrogates the experience and aftermath of colonisation, reclaiming voice and history.

questions.q: A 'new historicist' reading of a literary text would most characteristically:
options: judge the text purely by its formal elegance and unity
treat the text as one of many cultural documents circulating within and shaping the power relations of its period
focus only on the reader's emotional response
read the text as a timeless expression of universal human nature
questions.explain: New historicism situates a text among the period's other discourses, reading literature and history as mutually constitutive.

questions.q: The danger of 'context as bolt-on' refers to:
options: Analysing the poem's form
Using context to deepen interpretation
Pasting in historical or biographical information that does not actually illuminate the text's meaning
Comparing two texts
questions.explain: Bolt-on context is irrelevant background dropped in without connecting to how the text creates meaning.

questions.q: Sassoon's satirical war poems differ from Owen's elegiac mode chiefly through their:
options: Tender pity and hushed tones
Bitter irony and savage attack on those who prolonged the war from safety
Pastoral celebration of the home front
Refusal to mention soldiers
questions.explain: Sassoon often deploys biting irony to indict generals, politicians and complacent civilians.

questions.q: When two texts are compared, a 'point of divergence' is most valuable when it:
options: reveals how each writer handles a shared concern differently, illuminating both
repeats a similarity already noted
proves one text is superior
shows the texts are completely unrelated
questions.explain: Productive comparison uses difference to sharpen understanding of each text's distinctive method and meaning.

questions.q: A post-colonial reading of a canonical text might 'write back' by:
options: Removing all context
Exposing the text's imperial assumptions or giving voice to the colonised perspective it marginalised
Focusing only on metre
Praising the empire uncritically
questions.explain: 'Writing back' challenges imperial viewpoints and recovers the perspectives empire silenced.

questions.q: A 'psychoanalytic' (Freudian) reading would typically attend to:
options: the economic base determining the cultural superstructure
the text's fidelity to historical fact
the rhythm and metre of the verse alone
the unconscious, repression, desire and symbolic expressions of inner conflict
questions.explain: Psychoanalytic criticism reads texts for unconscious drives, repression and symbolic enactments of psychic conflict.

questions.q: 'Protest' or political writing is characterised by its intention to:
options: Avoid all reference to society
Entertain without any social purpose
Challenge injustice, power or oppression and provoke the reader to question the status quo
Describe nature for its own sake
questions.explain: Protest literature is purposive, contesting injustice and inviting critique of prevailing power.

questions.q: Modernism as a literary context responds to 'modern times' by registering:
options: Indifference to changing society
A return to medieval romance
A sense of fragmentation, alienation and the breakdown of old certainties after industrialisation and war
Confidence in steady moral and social progress
questions.explain: Modernist writing reflects a fractured, disorientating modernity, often through fragmented form and alienated voices.

questions.q: In close reading, attending to 'syntax' means examining:
options: the arrangement and ordering of words into sentence structures and their effects
the historical period of the text
the choice of individual words for connotation
the rhyme scheme of a stanza
questions.explain: Syntax concerns sentence structure and word order, whose patterning shapes pace, emphasis and meaning.

questions.q: When applying context, the strongest essays treat historical material as:
options: A fixed set of facts to be recited at the start
A substitute for reading the text
Decoration with no analytical purpose
A lens that illuminates specific choices of language, form and meaning in the text
questions.explain: Context works best as an interpretive lens tied to particular textual details, not recitation.

questions.q: Which is the best example of using context (AO3) analytically rather than as 'bolted-on' background?
options: A paragraph narrating the author's biography before discussing the text
Stating that the text was written in the nineteenth century
Showing how the poem's anxieties about industrialisation shape its imagery of the polluted river
Listing the dates of the period at the essay's start
questions.explain: Context is used well when it illuminates specific textual choices rather than sitting as detached background.

questions.q: Recognising that an interpretation is itself shaped by the critic's context means accepting that:
options: Criticism is unaffected by ideology
Critical readings (e.g. Marxist, feminist, post-colonial) reflect particular values and questions
There is only one timeless 'correct' reading
Context applies only to authors
questions.explain: Critical approaches are themselves historically and ideologically situated, generating different readings.

questions.q: Which sentence best demonstrates an integrated, analytical (rather than descriptive) point?
options: The character is angry in this scene.
Anger is a theme that appears in the text.
This passage is about anger and conflict.
The clipped monosyllables and end-stopped lines enact the speaker's controlled rage, refusing the release that fuller rhythm would allow.
questions.explain: Analytical writing links a precise technique to its effect on meaning, rather than merely naming a theme.

questions.q: A 'reader-response' approach holds that meaning is:
options: irrelevant to literary study
fixed entirely by the author's stated intention
produced in the interaction between the text and the reader's act of interpretation
determined solely by the historical context of composition
questions.explain: Reader-response criticism locates meaning in the transaction between text and reader rather than in the author alone.

questions.q: The 'changing role of women' as a shared context allows study of how literature reflects and shapes shifts in:
options: Astronomical discovery
Women's social, legal and economic status across periods
Military tactics only
The chemistry of dyes
questions.explain: Texts can be read against evolving expectations, rights and roles of women over time.

questions.q: A 'post-colonial' reading is most concerned with:
options: the recurrence of a single image
metre and rhyme scheme
representations of empire, the colonised 'other', hybridity and cultural power
the purging of pity and fear in the audience
questions.explain: Post-colonial criticism interrogates how texts construct empire, the colonised subject and relations of cultural power.

questions.q: To say a text is shaped by its 'context of production' is to consider:
options: Only how modern readers respond to it
The historical, social and personal circumstances in which it was written
The price of the first edition
Its print font
questions.explain: Context of production concerns the conditions under which a work was created, distinct from its later reception.

questions.q: In narrative theory, 'free indirect discourse' is best defined as:
options: a first-person narrator addressing the reader directly
a character's thoughts rendered in the third person yet inflected with that character's own idiom and feeling
an authorial commentary that judges the characters explicitly
direct speech reported within quotation marks
questions.explain: Free indirect discourse blends the narrator's third-person report with a character's voice, blurring the line between the two.

questions.q: A response that explores how a text can sustain feminist, Marxist and psychoanalytic readings is primarily demonstrating which assessment objective?
options: AO5
AO4
AO3
AO2
questions.explain: AO5 rewards engagement with different interpretations, including the application of distinct critical lenses.
